issue_context.title: TOB-K8S-016: Unsafe JSON construction
issue_context.body:
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Description**
Kubernetes uses JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) and similarly structured data sources throughout the codebase. This supports inter-component communications, both internally and externally to the cluster. However, a number of locations within the codebase use unsafe methods of constructing JSON:

```
pkg/kubectl/cmd/taint/taint.go:218:				conflictTaint := fmt.Sprintf("{\"%s\":\"%s\"}", taintRemove.Key, taintRemove.Effect)

pkg/apis/rbac/helpers.go:109:	formatString := "{" + strings.Join(formatStringParts, ", ") + "}"
```
Figure 24.1: Examples of incorrect JSON and JSON-like construction

**Exploit Scenario**
Alice runs a Kubernetes cluster in her organization. Bob, a user in Alice’s organization, attempts to add an RBAC permission that he is not entitled to, which causes his entire RBAC construction to be written to logs, and potentially improperly consumed elsewhere.

**Recommendation**
Short term, use proper format-specific encoders for all areas of the application, regardless of where the information is used. 

Long term, unify the encoding method to ensure encoded values are validated before use, and that no portion of the application produces values with different validations.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

See #81146 for current status of all issues created from these findings.

The vendor gave this issue an ID of TOB-K8S-016 and it was finding 26 of the report.

The vendor considers this issue Low Severity.

To view the original finding, begin on page 69 of the [Kubernetes Security Review Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Environment**:

- Kubernetes version: 1.13.4
comments: not sure about the other locations, but pkg/apis/rbac/helpers.go:109 is not producing JSON
nor is pkg/kubectl/cmd/taint/taint.go
both of those locations are logging human-readable messages, not parseable output

I am confused here.  The exploit cited in the opening comment,
> Alice runs a Kubernetes cluster in her organization. Bob, a user in Alice’s organization, attempts to add an RBAC permission that he is not entitled to, which causes his entire RBAC construction to be written to logs, and potentially improperly consumed elsewhere.

... has nothing to do with JSON construction; that exploit is about logging too much well-formed information.  I see associated PRs, such as #104064, that are changing the code that marshals data that is not security sensitive and will get logged anyway.

I did not have access to the security report. I am going by the short term recommendation and previous patches on the issue which basically asks us to encode all json properly. Please let me know if I missed anything.

@manugupt1 : I'll bet you _do_ have access, the problem is that the location of the audit materials has changed.  The relevant document and section reference is now https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/community/master/sig-security/security-audit-2019/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf#h.ovfpcse8zb7i .  This particular "finding" is pretty unimpressive, to my taste.  The cited exploit is not on point at all.  The first cited code example _might_ be vulnerable to syntax injection attacks --- or might not; it depends on the sources of the strings involved.  I could certainly support replacing `\"%s\"` in the format string with `%q`; that is a rather cheap and tiny change.  The second cited code example does not show anything about the data involved.

What is meant by the following recommendation?
> Long term, unify the encoding method to ensure encoded values are validated before use, 
and that no portion of the application produces values with different validations.

There are two levels of validation.  One is done by the JSON parser.  Another is done (a) in the registered type-specific code for types defined in the original way and (b) I suppose by an openapi schema driven validator for types defined by a CRD.  Without a relevant exploit or other explanation, it is hard to know what the concern or recommendation here is.  Addressing the type-specific validation would be --- well, I do not even know what it would be.  We are often talking about code that is generating patches, and we have only marshaling and validation for whole objects rather than patches.  And the apiserver _does_ validate the whole objects before use.  Addressing the JSON-level validation (which is the activity I see) --- how is that different from the short-term recommendation?

@MikeSpreitzer I did not know this existed in the archives as well. I think the finding itself may not be useful. 

When I was thinking about this, I had the same thoughts. However, I think it is still better for us create objects for json wherever possible rather than creating the string manually. LMK what do you think.
